subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the area of the region bounded by y = x³ + 3, the x-axis and the lines x = −1, x = 2.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book printed p.102 — Star Q+ share, under the banner 'DEFINITE INTEGRALS-VSAQ', answer 216, the first of three area questions on this page. Printed appearance: TS 19. Chapter star rank ★★★ applies (Star Q+ entries take their chapter-section's rank). No margin mark tags are printed, so the 1+1+2 split is OURS, patterned on the 1+1+2 shape already used for this unit's other AREA questions (e.g. ts_ipe_m2b_di_saq_area_y_eq_x2_and_y_eq_x3 in the printed SAQ chapter). We classify this answer as SAQ shape, not VSAQ (the book's page header says 'VSAQ' for the whole 212–218 run, but a three-step area derivation matches the 4-mark SAQ form used elsewhere in this book, not a 2-mark VSAQ) — this classification is OURS. No figure is authored: y=x³+3 never crosses the x-axis on [−1,2] (it is already +2 at x=−1), so there is no boundary or sign-change picture to draw and the algebra is self-contained. Boundary reading: printed p.100 confirms the Hyperbola Star Q+ share ends at answer 211; printed p.103 confirms the Bullet Model Paper begins at Q1&2 Circles — so this chapter's Star Q+ share is exactly answers 212–218. insider_note: Because the curve never crosses the x-axis on this interval, this question is simpler than it first looks — the only care needed is checking the sign before integrating, which the book itself does not show explicitly.

steps.label: Set up the area integral
steps.margin_note: First mark. Confirm y stays positive on the whole interval before writing down a single, unsplit integral.
steps.memory_tip: x³+3 is increasing, and its smallest value on [−1,2] is at x=−1, where it is already +2 — so it never dips below the x-axis.
lines: So the curve stays above the x-axis over
steps.why: Since y=x³+3 is positive at both ends of the interval and is a strictly increasing function, it never crosses the x-axis on [−1,2], so the area under the curve is simply the plain definite integral with no sign-splitting needed.
common_mistakes: Splitting the integral at x=0 out of habit, which is unnecessary here since the curve never goes negative.
Forgetting to check the sign of y before setting up the integral.

steps.label: Find the antiderivative
steps.margin_note: Second mark. x⁴/4 + 3x is the antiderivative — check both terms are present before substituting limits.
steps.memory_tip: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) — increase the power by one and divide by the new power.
steps.why: Integrating x³ term by term gives x⁴/4, and integrating the constant 3 gives 3x, so the antiderivative is x⁴/4+3x.
common_mistakes: Integrating x³ incorrectly as x⁴ without dividing by 4.
Forgetting the +3x term from the constant part of the integrand.

steps.label: Apply the limits and simplify
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. Subtracting a negative value at x=−1 turns the subtraction into an addition.
steps.memory_tip: (−1)⁴ = 1, not −1 — an even power of a negative number is always positive.
steps.why: Substituting x=2 gives 16/4+6=10, and substituting x=−1 gives 1/4−3=−11/4; subtracting the lower value from the upper value (10 minus a negative) adds the two magnitudes together, giving 51/4.
common_mistakes: Losing the sign when subtracting the negative lower-limit value −11/4.
An arithmetic slip converting 10 to the fraction 40/4 before adding 11/4.
